title: Listening as love
hookLine: listening may be love's most common form

cards: Halfway through a friend's story, a sentence starts forming. A better story. A piece of advice.
The same thing happened to me. The friend is still talking, but the mind has already left the room to rehearse.
It's a moment with two sides: the one waiting to speak, and the one who can tell they're not really being heard.
Two old texts, from the letter of James and from the book of Job, point at another way to be in a conversation.

teach.h: SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.
teach.b: First, the order of things. The letter of James, in the King James Bible, puts it in a single line: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Swift to hear comes first.
Not clever to answer. Not quick with advice. The ears come ahead of the mouth.

Second, a picture of it done well. In the book of Job, everything has been taken from Job: his children, his health, his wealth. Three friends come to comfort him, and at first they do something remarkable.

teach.h: THEY SAT WITH HIM ON THE GROUND.
teach.b: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." They don't explain. They don't fix.
They stay. Third, what happens next. Eventually the friends start talking, for chapters, explaining why this must have happened to him.

teach.h: WRONG WHEN THEY STARTED TO SPEAK.
teach.b: Some readers notice that the friends were at their best in the silence, and went wrong when they started to speak. At the end of the book, the text says God is not pleased with what they said about him.
Fourth, a word from Hebrew that holds all of this.
A prayer said in Jewish worship, from the book of Deuteronomy, begins with Shema: hear, or listen. In that prayer, listening comes first.
Listening isn't a pause before the real love begins. It can be the love. Full attention says, without a single word, you matter enough for me to stop.

how: Jews say the Shema, which opens with the word hear, in daily prayer; in Jewish mourning, by custom, visitors to a house of mourning wait for the mourner to speak first, and people on many paths practice listening as a form of care in chaplaincy and friendship.

games.q: who listened, and how — tap the pairs.
p: swift to hear, slow to speak
sat on the ground and said nothing

s: James says to be swift to speak and slow to hear
it's the other way round: "swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath."
Job's friends first sat with him in silence
"none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great."

games.q: you're one of Job's friends. you've just arrived and found him sitting in ruin. what do you do?
o: explain why this happened to him.
sit on the ground with him and say nothing.
games.why: they sit with him seven days and seven nights, and none speak a word. some readers say it was the best thing they did.

practice: Close your eyes, or let them rest low, and just listen: first the farthest sound you can hear, then something closer in the room, then the closest of all, your own breath, letting each arrive and leave without naming or judging it.
When your mind starts composing something to say, notice it and come back to listening, the same muscle a friend needs from you. If you pray, you can listen in your own tradition's way.

wordCard.voice: Shema. The opening word of a Jewish prayer that means hear, or listen, placing attention before any answer. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: hear, or listen, the first word of the Shema, a prayer from Deuteronomy said in Jewish worship.

carryVoice: Your line: just listen. Sometimes the kindest answer is your full attention. See you tomorrow.
